title: California Leaders Honor Jane Goodall After Passing of Trailblazing Primatologist at 91 - NewsBreak
text:
4 hours ago SACRAMENTO – Governor Gavin Newsom and First Partner Jennifer Siebel Newsom issued a statement Wednesday mourning the death of Jane Goodall, the world-renowned primatologist and environmentalist who once received the California Museum’s Minerva Award.
Photo by Governor's Press Office “Jane Goodall was a global legend – a woman known for her extraordinary empathy and her remarkable intellect. She stood at the forefront of discovery, breaking through barriers for women in primatology, in science, and beyond. Jane’s curiosity, strength, and kindness changed the world, and inspired countless people and bridged countries and cultures in pursuit of a better future. To us she was a towering inspiration, and a cherished friend. Her commitment to animals, the environment, and the world as a whole, led her to found institutions and programs that will carry on her legacy for decades,” the governor and first partner said.
The Jane Goodall Institute, based in Washington, D.C., confirmed her passing in an Instagram post, saying the 91-year-old conservationist died of natural causes while in California during a U.S. speaking tour. “Her discoveries revolutionized science, and she was a tireless advocate for the protection and restoration of our natural world,” the institute said.
Goodall first rose to prominence in the 1960s while living among chimpanzees in Africa, where she documented their use of tools and social bonds once thought to be uniquely human. Her pioneering research reshaped the scientific community’s understanding of animals and introduced millions of people to the emotional depth of wildlife.
Through her travels, documentaries, and tireless advocacy, Goodall became a household name and a voice for conservation across generations. Her legacy endures through the institutions she founded and the global movement she inspired to protect animals and the planet.
